analysis.one_liner: Requires drug maker rebates to be passed to patients at the pharmacy counter and limits pharmacy middleman pay to transparent flat fees.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate health committee; it was referred there on March 30, 2023 and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the current system, drug makers pay large rebates to pharmacy benefit managers and insurers, and patients often pay the full list price at the pharmacy while the rebate is kept or passed back later. This bill would make those rebates illegal unless the discount shows up in the price the patient actually pays at the counter, and it would let middlemen be paid only flat, transparent service fees instead of a share of the rebate money. It would cover both Medicare and private insurance plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay coinsurance or a percentage of a drug's list price. Today, when a rebate goes back to the insurer or middleman, the patient's out-of-pocket charge is still calculated off the higher list price. Forcing the discount to appear at the point of sale would lower what patients actually pay at the pharmacy. Employers and plans would also see the full price picture, and Medicare Part D beneficiaries would get the same protection.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strips the federal safe harbor that currently allows drug makers to pay rebates to insurers and pharmacy benefit managers without violating anti-kickback law, unless the rebate is reflected in the price the patient pays at the pharmacy [S2, S3].

It applies the same rule to private insurance through the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code, so group health plans and their pharmacy benefit managers cannot accept manufacturer rebates unless the discount reaches the enrollee at the point of sale [S3].

Any other money a pharmacy benefit manager takes from a drug maker must be a flat, transparent service fee paid for actual services, so middlemen can no longer be paid a cut of a hidden price spread [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers lose the rebate revenue and the price spread they currently keep, and drug makers would have to restructure how they price and discount drugs. Consumers could see some premium changes during the transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy middlemen, insurers, and drug makers

drawbacks.text: Rebates currently flow back to plans and help offset premiums for everyone, including members who use no prescriptions; forcing rebates to the point of sale shifts that money to pharmacy customers, so premiums could rise for some people even as drug counter prices fall.

The flat-fee exception still lets pharmacy benefit managers stay in business and negotiate on behalf of plans, and leaves the Secretary of Health and Human Services to define the conditions, so much of the protection depends on how the rules are written and enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — the patient sees the discount at the counter instead of the middleman pocketing it — directly targets a well-documented reason patients overpay at the pharmacy. The honest cost is that premiums, which are shared by people who use few prescriptions, may absorb part of the shift, and the flat-fee structure depends heavily on future regulation. On balance the bill moves money from hidden intermediaries to the patients who fill the prescriptions, but it is not free for premium payers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the Drug Price Transparency Act of 2023 on March 30, 2023, with Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as cosponsor [S1, S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded: no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll call [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and insurers keep the rebate system untouched, since the bill never advanced. Patients who would have seen discounts at the pharmacy counter are no better off than before.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require drug rebates to reach patients at the point of sale.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee where the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; it received no markup, no vote, and no report after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Republican senators were attached to the bill and no votes were ever taken, so there is no record of where the parties stood.

industries.note: These middlemen negotiate rebates from drug makers and are paid through a share of the hidden price spread. The bill would end that pay model, allowing only flat, transparent service fees, and covers affiliated entities under common ownership so the big vertically integrated PBMs are reached [S3].

Plans currently receive manufacturer rebates and many insurers own PBMs, so they lose both the rebate money and the middleman profits. They would also gain price transparency for the plans they administer, but the largest effect is losing rebate revenue.

Drug makers would lose the rebate system they use to win favorable placement on insurers' drug lists. They might respond by lowering list prices, which benefits patients at the counter, but they would also lose a tool for steering formulary decisions.
